{{Short description|American mathematician (1875–1952)}}
'''Ralph Ernest Powers''' (April 27, 1875 – January 31, 1952) was an American amateur mathematician who worked on [[prime numbers]].

He is credited with discovering the [[Mersenne prime]]s {{math|''M''<sub>89</sub>}} and {{math|''M''<sub>107</sub>}}, in 1911 and 1914 respectively.<ref>{{cite journal |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |title=The Tenth Perfect Number |author=R. E. Powers |volume= 18 |issue=11 |pages=195–197 |year=1911 |jstor=2972574 |quote=The article is signed "DENVER, COLORADO, June, 1911" |doi=10.2307/2972574}}</ref><ref>[http://plms.oxfordjournals.org/content/s2-13/1/1.1.full.pdf ]{{dead link|date=May 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} Proc. London Math. Soc. (1914) s2–13 (1): 1. Result presented at a meeting with London Mathematical Society on June 11, 1914. Retrieved 2016-04-17.</ref> In 1934 he verified that the Mersenne number {{math|''M''<sub>241</sub>}} is composite.<ref>{{cite journal |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |title=Note on a Mersenne Number |author=R. E. Powers |volume= 40 |issue=12 |year=1934 |page=883 |doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1934-05994-9|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Life==
Powers was born in [[Fountain, Colorado|Fountain, Colorado Territory]]. Details of his life are little-known,<ref name="obituary">[https://www.ams.org/journals/mcom/1952-06-038/S0025-5718-52-99396-4/S0025-5718-52-99396-4.pdf Obituary] by [[Derrick Henry Lehmer|D. H. Lehmer]]</ref> though he appears to have been an employee of the [[Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad]].<ref name="Williams1998">{{cite book|author=Hugh C. Williams|title=Édouard Lucas and Primality Testing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9MxmRntmJF4C|year=1998|publisher=Wiley|isbn=978-0-471-14852-4}}</ref>

Soon after Powers announced the discovery of {{math|''M''<sub>107</sub>}}, the Frenchman E. Fauquembergue claimed that he had discovered it earlier, but many of Fauquembergue's other claims were later demonstrated as erroneous; thus, many prefer recognizing Powers as the discoverer, including the well-known Internet resource the [[PrimePages]].

After his own discoveries of Mersenne primes in 1911 and 1914, no [[Mersenne primes]] were discovered until [[Raphael M. Robinson]] used a computer to find the next two, on January 30, 1952, the night before Powers's death.<ref name="obituary" />

==Works==
* ‘The Tenth Perfect Number', ''American Mathematical Monthly'', Vol. 18 (1911), pp.&nbsp;195–7
* ’On Mersenne's Numbers', ''Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society'', Vol. 13 (1914), p. xxxix
* 'A Mersenne Prime', ''Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society'', Vol. 20, No. 10 (1914), p.&nbsp;531
* ’Certain composite Mersenne's numbers', ''Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society'' Vol. 15 (1916), p. xxii
* (with [[D. H. Lehmer]]) 'On Factoring Large Numbers', ''Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society'', Vol. 37. No. 10 (1931), pp.&nbsp;770–76
* ’Note on a Mersenne Number', ''Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society'', Vol. 40, No. 12 (1934), p.&nbsp;883
